text: I’ll first inspect the STEP declaration and import it with OCCT, then report its topology, dimensions, and validity before choosing a fluid-volume extraction strategy.

The file explicitly declares metres, contains three valid solids, and spans 53.95 × 46.29 × 31.30 m. I’ll now render the three solids separately and inspect their overlap/arrangement; this determines whether they are wall parts enclosing a void or nested solids from which the fluid can be extracted.

The solids form stacked, partly overlapping housing components rather than nested “fluid” and “wall” bodies. I’ll inspect each component independently from a common viewpoint and section-like side views to identify ports and the enclosed passage.

The parts resemble a lower cover, an upper circular insert, and a surrounding casing. To avoid guessing from appearance, I’ll inspect the STEP product names and OCCT topology hierarchy, which may identify components and distinguish a fan/rotor from enclosure parts.
I’ll examine horizontal cross-sections through the assembled parts. These sections should reveal the internal void, its openings, and whether the “EMITTER” occupies or bounds the airflow passage.
One slice contained no intersection and the plotting call rejected the empty result. I’ll repeat with an explicit empty-section check so the inspection is reproducible.

The sections show that `BODY` and `EMITTER` are volumetric regions, not thin casing shells. I’ll quantify their contacts and overlaps. If their union is one connected solid, the STEP is likely already a multi-part representation of the internal flow volume; if not, it is a material assembly requiring cavity extraction.
The first pair has no Boolean common and OCCT returns `None` for that case. I’ll handle empty intersections explicitly and repeat the connectivity test.

The parts only touch at interfaces and do not enclose a separate void; the `BODY` itself is almost the full rounded-square prism. I’ll inspect planar end faces and interface areas to determine whether the assembly represents a split positive flow volume (with end caps as inlet/outlet) rather than wall material.

The interfaces match exactly: `BASE` top to `BODY` bottom, and `BODY` top to `EMITTER` bottom (the latter both 1392.883 m² at z = 20.1 m). There is no enclosed void between material shells. I will therefore treat the three touching STEP solids as the split positive flow volume, fuse them without rescaling (STEP declares metres), and use the outer BASE bottom as inlet and outer EMITTER top as outlet. I’ll test the OCC fuse and inspect the resulting boundary before meshing.

OCC preserves two touching volumes because one interface is purely coincident, but Boolean fragmentation has made that interface conformal. I’ll inspect volume masses, shared faces, and exact top boundary faces. The mesh can then combine both conformal volumes into one OpenFOAM cell region while excluding shared interfaces from external patches.

The attempted tangential fuse produced an invalid nested BREP, so I will not use it. Instead I’ll fragment the original three valid solids to obtain a conformal multi-volume tetrahedral mesh and place all resulting cells in one physical fluid region. The shared CAD interfaces will remain internal faces, while only exterior faces receive inlet/outlet/wall patches. A coarse 1.5 m target size will suppress the sub-cell fillet detail rather than forcing cells around it.

The coarse Gmsh mesh was written, but the bookkeeping print failed after meshing, so that cell is not replay-safe. I’ll immediately repeat the same conformal fragmentation at a coarser 2.5 m target, finish cleanly, and leave a reproducible `fluid.msh` on disk.
I’ll re-emit the successful coarse mesh cell with its missing `Counter` import included, making it valid when `build.py` is replayed from empty.
The coarsest tetrahedral mesh now exists reproducibly. I’ll convert it to OpenFOAM and inspect the converter’s region and patch output before rendering or refining.
OpenFOAM requires a minimal case dictionary even for mesh conversion. I’ll create only that mesh-infrastructure file—no solver setup or boundary conditions.
I’ll rerun the converter now that the minimal case structure exists.

Conversion produced 15,173 tetrahedra and the requested named patches, but also 5,534 `defaultFaces`. These may be the unassigned internal CAD interfaces or a true patching defect. I’ll run `checkMesh` now to distinguish them and assess topology and cell quality.
This OpenFOAM build loads `fvSchemes` for the extended geometry checks. I’ll add empty mesh-utility dictionaries only; still no physics or boundary conditions.
I’ll rerun the full topology and geometry check.

The mesh is topologically one region and closed, but it fails five quality checks because sub-millimetric CAD edges are being honored in a 2.5 m mesh (minimum edge 3.7×10⁻⁷ m). This is exactly the fillet/detail issue in the request. I’ll heal each imported solid with a 0.10 m small-edge/small-face tolerance (4% of the chosen cell size), then remesh with Delaunay tetrahedra. This preserves the declared overall dimensions while removing geometry that cannot survive the coarse mesh.

The healed geometry retains three conformal volumes and has fewer exterior faces. I’ll reconvert it and run the binding mesh check to see whether the 0.10 m defeaturing removed the pathological cells.

OCC healing did not remove the microscopic edge defects and also dropped the BASE cells from the physical volume, so I will not keep that mesh. I’ll switch to a coarse Cartesian cut-cell approximation of the imported positive volume: classify 1.5 m Cartesian cell centers against the three original valid solids, retain occupied cells, and preserve the exact z = 0 and z = 31.3 end planes. This intentionally removes all sub-cell fillets and avoids CAD-sliver tetrahedra. First I’ll verify OCCT point classification at known interior/exterior points.

Point classification confirms the three solids occupy successive stacked portions of one flow volume. I’ll now generate the coarse Cartesian OpenFOAM mesh directly from that imported geometry, with end-plane boundary faces named at creation and every other exposed face assigned to `walls`.

The Cartesian mesh contains 12,545 cells and preserves the exact declared end planes. I’ll now run the full OpenFOAM check; if it passes, I’ll render the boundary and a cutaway to verify the coarse shape and patch placement.

The Cartesian topology is correct, but five of the six local face templates were wound inward; only the +z face was correct. I’ll reverse those templates in the already generated face list and rewrite `faces`, preserving all connectivity and patch assignments.
I’ll rerun the binding check after correcting face orientation.

The corrected mesh passes all checks except 53 under-determined cells. These are one-cell remnants of sub-grid tabs/fillets with neighbors spanning fewer than three independent directions. I’ll prune only those unsupported Cartesian cells, iterating until every retained cell has a three-dimensional neighbor stencil, then rewrite the mesh. This is the explicit sub-cell feature removal step.
I’ll run the full mesh check on the pruned Cartesian mesh.

The final coarse mesh passes all topology and geometry checks: one connected region, 12,467 orthogonal hexahedra, three patches, and no failed checks. I’ll render its exterior and a cutaway, coloring the inlet and outlet by their exact end planes to visually confirm the shape and flow openings.
